question: Are async:true command hooks for the status events non-blocking, and do they leave the model request byte-identical?

2.1.317.method: The same scripted session (a plain turn, an allowed Bash tool call, a second plain turn) ran once per configuration against a local stub. Every /v1/messages body was normalised (per-profile device id and session id inside metadata.user_id, uuids, tool ids, timestamps, ports and the run folder name replaced) and compared with the no-hook run, request by request, byte for byte. The time from Enter to the first model request that follows it was read from one clock.

base2.configuration: no hooks, second run (the noise floor of the comparison)

http.configuration: http hooks for the C-2 event list, receiver answers {}

cmd.configuration: node command hook, synchronous, no delay

cmdsync-d2.configuration: node command hook, synchronous, the hook process stays alive 2000 ms

cmdasync-d2.configuration: node command hook with async:true, stays alive 2000 ms, prints nothing

ps.configuration: the product's integration/claude-hook.ps1 as today (UserPromptSubmit, Stop, Notification, PermissionRequest synchronous; tool events async)

psasync.configuration: the product's claude-hook.ps1 with async:true on every C-2 event (what command-async would be)

permissionDialogCheck.note: A second session with a Write that needs the owner (dialog) and key 1: with every C-2 event async the dialog still drew, the owner key still answered, and the four model requests are still identical to the no-hook run.

summary: Yes in both versions. A command hook that stays alive for 2 s delays the model request by about 2 s when it is synchronous and by nothing measurable when async:true. The model requests of every hook configuration (http, sync command, async command, the product PowerShell hook sync and async) are identical to the no-hook run after normalisation, and the no-hook run is identical to a second no-hook run, so the comparison has no noise of its own. Output of {} from an async hook changes nothing either.
caveats: Windows only: the product PowerShell hook and the named pipe do not exist elsewhere. E1 must not enable command-async on POSIX until a CI capture covers the bash and zsh wrappers.
Async hooks here print nothing or {}. A hook that prints systemMessage or additionalContext was not measured because Agentrix never does that for status events.
Milliseconds are observations from one Windows 11 machine, taken with nothing else running. They show an order of magnitude, they are not test bounds.
Normalisation hides only the per-profile device and session id; every other byte of the system prompt, the tool list and the messages was compared.
